notes: Bhutan has no legal parties in 1970: slots are filled with the crown, state institutions (Tshogdu, Council of Ministers, Zhung Dratshang, army, police, forest service), the Dorji family, the exiled Bhutan State Congress and cross-border parties active among Nepali-speakers on the southern border (Nepali Congress, CPI, CPI(M), CPI(ML)). Bhutan State Congress placed in 18 (has popularity) rather than 3; Zhung Dratshang in 14 as church-based conservatism outside the blocs. Islamic slots use Indian Muslim networks reaching the southern border bazaars, as Bhutan itself has almost no Muslims.

0.name: Bhutan House
0.text:
Bhutan House in Kalimpong is the seat of the Dorji family, the kingdom's hereditary agents in British India, who ran its administration and foreign dealings for half a century. Their power broke in April 1964 with the assassination of Lonchen Jigme Palden Dorji; his brother Lhendup Dorji, briefly acting Lonchen, fled to Nepal in 1965. The matriarch Rani Chuni Dorji still presides in Kalimpong, and her daughter Ashi Kesang is queen.

The family stands for modernisation directed by an anglicised elite: centralised administration, Western schooling, an opening to the wider world and less deference to both the monk body and New Delhi. Its leverage lies in wealth, Calcutta and London connections and blood ties to the throne.

1.name: Gyelyong Tshogdu
1.text:
The National Assembly was created by Jigme Dorji Wangchuck in 1953 and meets in Thimphu twice a year. Most members are chimis chosen by the villages, joined by representatives of the monk body and officials nominated by the crown. In 1968 the king renounced his veto over its resolutions, and the assembly can now dismiss ministers and even force the monarch to abdicate by a two-thirds vote.

Its temper is cautious and royalist: the chimis guard village interests, taxes and labour levies, debate the settlement of Nepali immigrants in the south and endorse the king's measured opening to India and the United Nations. Its leverage is legitimacy, as the only national forum where commoners speak to the throne.

2.name: Colombo Plan Scholars
2.text:
Bhutan's first generation of modern-educated officials, schooled at the mission schools of Kalimpong and Darjeeling and in Indian colleges, and increasingly trained abroad since Bhutan joined the Colombo Plan in 1962. They staff the ministries created in 1968, the offices of the Five-Year Plans and the young foreign service, and they owe their careers to the king's reforms.

They favour a professional civil service, codified law, wider English-medium schooling, membership of the United Nations and a broader circle of donors beyond India. They lack any mass base, but they draft the files, budgets and treaties of a state that can no longer function without them.

3.name: Nepali Congress
3.text:
Nepal's democratic party, banned in its homeland since King Mahendra's royal coup of 1960, operates from exile in India. Its leader B. P. Koirala, released from prison in 1968, directs the party from Banaras and courts Nepali-speaking communities across the Himalayan foothills, including the Lhotshampa settlers of southern Bhutan, whose own Bhutan State Congress was modelled on it.

It stands for parliamentary democracy, land reform and democratic socialism in the Socialist International mould, and it is firmly anti-communist. In Bhutan its pull is indirect: through Nepali-language papers, teachers and kin networks in Darjeeling and Assam it keeps alive the idea that southern farmers deserve elected representation and equal citizenship.

4.name: Communist Party of India
4.text:
India's pro-Moscow communist party, led by general secretary C. Rajeswara Rao since the 1964 split, organises plantation workers in the Duars tea gardens and Nepali-speaking labourers in the Darjeeling hills, right along Bhutan's southern border. Its cadres reach the Lhotshampa through kinship, cross-border markets and the labour gangs building Bhutan's roads.

It preaches Soviet-style socialism, trade unionism and anti-feudal reform, and it denounces Bhutan's monarchy and compulsory labour levies as relics of serfdom. Inside the kingdom it has no organisation and no legal footing; its leverage depends on India's own politics and on discontent among southern workers and tenants.

5.name: Communist Party of India (Marxist–Leninist)
5.text:
Founded on 22 April 1969 by Charu Majumdar, the party grew out of the 1967 peasant uprising at Naxalbari in the Siliguri corridor, not far from Bhutan's southern border. Its Naxalite squads are spreading across Bengal, and Thimphu watches their appeal to Nepali-speaking and Adivasi tea-garden labour with alarm.

It rejects elections, glorifies Mao Zedong's people's war and calls for the annihilation of landlords and class enemies. In Bhutan it has no cells, but it is the court's nightmare: a guerrilla creed that could travel up the southern foothills among landless Lhotshampa tenants and road labourers.

6.name: Chhoesi Nyiden
6.text:
The Zhabdrung Rinpoche, reincarnation of Bhutan's seventeenth-century founder, was once the country's spiritual sovereign. The Wangchuck monarchy has kept the line at arm's length since 1907; the previous incarnation died in obscure circumstances at Talo in 1931, and the boy recognised as the current one, Jigme Ngawang Namgyal, fled to India in 1962. Around him gather monks, lay devotees and families who never accepted a hereditary throne.

They want the old dual system restored under the Zhabdrung: religious authority above secular power, the monk body supreme, and modernisation, foreign aid and outside influence held at bay. Their leverage is spiritual prestige in the western valleys and the throne's lingering unease about the boy in exile.

7.name: Royal Bhutan Police
7.text:
Formed on 1 September 1965 from army detachments, after the Lonchen's assassination and the attempt on the king's life, the Royal Bhutan Police guards the southern border towns, the checkpoints on the new highways and the capital. Raised with Indian help, it answers directly to the palace and the home administration.

Its creed is order: border control, surveillance of exiles and conspirators, policing of immigrant labour and suppression of any organised opposition. As the instrument that hunts plotters and watches the Lhotshampa south, it is the natural core of a harder security state should the court ever choose that road.

8.name: All India Shia Conference
8.text:
The All India Shia Conference, founded at Lucknow in 1907, speaks for India's Twelver Shia community. Through Shia merchants and contractors from Calcutta and Lucknow who trade in Phuntsholing, Samchi and Samdrup Jongkhar, its newspapers and charities reach the handful of Shia families living in Bhutan's southern border bazaars.

It is moderate and loyalist, seeking protection for mourning processions, religious endowments and schools, communal representation and good relations with whatever government rules. It looks to Lucknow and Najaf for religious guidance rather than political direction, and its leverage in Bhutan is limited to commerce and the goodwill of local officials.

9.name: Najafi Talaba
9.text:
A few Indian Shia seminarians back from the hawza of Najaf preach in the Shia quarters of Calcutta and now and then among the traders who move between Bengal and Bhutan's border markets. They follow Grand Ayatollah Muhsin al-Hakim and admire the exiled Ruhollah Khomeini, who has taught in Najaf since 1965.

They call for strict observance, clerical leadership of the community and rejection of secular and Western ways, and they regard kings of every kind with suspicion. In Bhutan they have no organisation and barely a dozen listeners; their only leverage lies in the trading networks that tie Calcutta to the southern bazaars.

10.name: Tablighi Jamaat
10.text:
The Tablighi Jamaat, the apolitical preaching movement founded in Mewat in 1926, sends touring groups of lay missionaries through the Muslim settlements of the Duars and Assam. Under its amir Muhammad Inamul Hasan, small parties of preachers occasionally reach Muslim shopkeepers, drivers and labourers in Bhutan's southern bazaars.

It shuns politics, preaches personal piety, prayer and correct ritual, and counsels obedience to established authority, which makes it the most accommodating of Islamic movements. In Bhutan it seeks only room to pray and preach among Indian Muslim workers; its leverage is its discipline and its tolerated, unthreatening presence.

11.name: Khilafat Halqa
11.text:
A tiny clandestine study circle among Bengali Muslim traders and itinerant preachers in the Duars border towns, nourished by memories of the Khilafat Movement and by pan-Islamic pamphlets carried in from East Pakistan. It has no known leader and meets in private homes rather than mosques.

Its members dream of a restored caliphate uniting all Muslims across the borders drawn in 1947, reject secular states and monarchies alike and regard the Himalayan kingdoms as lands of unbelief. In Bhutan it is all but invisible; its only leverage is secrecy and the open, lightly watched southern border.

12.name: Jamaat-e-Islami Hind
12.text:
The Indian branch of Abul A'la Maududi's movement, organised separately after partition, is led from Delhi by its amir Abul Lais Islahi Nadvi. Its units in West Bengal and Assam run study circles, literature and welfare work among Muslims along the northern frontier, including merchants who do business in Bhutan's border towns.

It seeks an Islamic moral order built through education, preaching and a disciplined cadre, accepts a role in public life and rejects both Western secularism and communism. It is cautious and legalistic, and its foothold in Bhutan is limited to a few readers among Indian Muslim traders in Phuntsholing and Gelephu.

13.name: Lhengye Zhungtshog
13.text:
The Council of Ministers was created by Jigme Dorji Wangchuck in 1968 to share the burden of rule after the office of Lonchen fell vacant. The king presides over it, and its ministers head the new departments of the royal government, working alongside the Royal Advisory Council, the Lodoe Tshogde, set up in 1965.

It embodies development without bloc alignment: Indian-financed Five-Year Plans, roads, schools and hospitals, membership of the Universal Postal Union in 1969 and a patient campaign for a seat at the United Nations. Its power rests on the king's confidence, control of the budget and a monopoly of expertise in a country without parties.

14.name: Zhung Dratshang
14.text:
The Central Monastic Body of the Drukpa Kagyu school is Bhutan's state religious establishment. Headed by the Je Khenpo, it winters in Punakha Dzong and summers in Thimphu's Tashichho Dzong, rebuilt by the king as the seat of government. It holds seats in the National Assembly and the Royal Advisory Council and is maintained from the royal treasury.

It defends Drukpa Buddhism as the soul of the nation, the monastic schools, the ritual calendar and the sanctity of the dzongs, and it watches secular education and foreign influence warily. Its leverage is immense: thousands of monks, deep village loyalty and the power to bless, or quietly withhold blessing from, the throne's reforms.

15.name: Bank of Bhutan
15.text:
Bhutan's first bank, founded by royal charter in 1968 at Phuntsholing, sits at the centre of a small but growing circle of wealth: noble families with large estates, contractors on Indian-funded road projects, timber and transport licensees and the trading houses of the southern border. Nearly all of this capital is tied to the court and its leading families.

The circle wants sound money on the Indian rupee, lucrative state contracts, protection of landed estates against further land ceilings and a slow, controlled opening to trade. It has no public voice, but in a cash-poor kingdom whoever holds the credit and the contracts quietly shapes the pace of development.

16.name: Phuntsholing Tshongpa
16.text:
The shopkeepers, transporters and small traders of Phuntsholing, Gelephu and Samdrup Jongkhar, Ngalop, Lhotshampa and Indian alike, form the kingdom's only bazaar economy. Phuntsholing, the gateway town on the Indian border, has boomed since the motor road to Thimphu opened in the early 1960s and the Bank of Bhutan set up there.

They want free movement of goods across the open border, low duties, fewer licences and permits, release from compulsory labour levies and secure title to town plots. Politically timid but economically indispensable, they gain with every new road, and the market they carry northward is a quiet challenge to the old order.

17.name: Department of Forests
17.text:
Founded in 1952, the Department of Forests is the royal government's guardian of a country still largely covered in forest. Under the Bhutan Forest Act of 1969 all forests have been brought under state ownership, and in 1966 the Manas wildlife sanctuary was set aside along the southern border with Assam.

Its foresters stand for conservation before exploitation: control of logging and timber exports to India, curbs on shifting cultivation, protection of watersheds and wildlife, and replanting. Its leverage comes from the king's personal interest, the new law of 1969 and a growing conviction in Thimphu that the forests are a national inheritance rather than a commodity.

18.name: Bhutan State Congress
18.text:
Founded in 1952 in Assam by Lhotshampa activists inspired by the Indian and Nepali Congress parties, the Bhutan State Congress led a failed satyagraha into southern Bhutan in 1954 and was banned. It survives in exile in Assam and West Bengal as a dwindling organisation, many of whose followers have made their peace with the throne since the Nationality Law of 1958.

It demands responsible government, equal citizenship and secure land rights for Nepali-speaking settlers, an end to forced labour and discriminatory taxes, and representation for the south. Its programme is democratic and broadly socialist; its leverage rests on southern grievances and on sympathetic patrons across the Indian border.

19.name: Communist Party of India (Marxist)
19.text:
Formed in the 1964 split and steering its own course between Moscow and Beijing, the Communist Party of India (Marxist) is the strongest party in West Bengal. Jyoti Basu is deputy chief minister in the United Front government in Calcutta, and general secretary P. Sundarayya directs a mass apparatus of unions and peasant associations reaching into the Duars.

It champions land redistribution, militant trade unionism and anti-imperialism while contesting elections. For Bhutan it matters as the governing force across the southern border, able to shelter dissidents and to organise the Nepali-speaking tea and transport workers whose kin live inside the kingdom.

20.name: Tsawa Sum
20.text:
A loose bloc of Ngalop chimis, district officials and village elders who rally around tsawa sum, the three roots of king, country and people. It has no formal organisation, but its voice dominates Tshogdu debates on Nepali immigration, land settlement in the south and the preservation of Drukpa dress, language and custom.

It wants immigration from Nepal halted, the southern settlers confined and assimilated, Dzongkha promoted as the national tongue and Drukpa culture made obligatory in public life. Fiercely loyal to the throne, it distrusts Indian influence and Western modernity alike; its leverage is the fear that the Drukpa could become a minority in their own land, as the Lepcha and Bhutia have in Sikkim.

21.name: Pazap
21.text:
A circle of veterans of the old regional militias, dzong retainers and young officers who romanticise the pazap, the warrior levies that fought the British in the Duar War of 1864–65. It has no leader of note and no formal existence, but its talk is heard in army messes and in the households of the old western nobility.

It calls for Drukpa supremacy, a nation in arms with universal militia service, the expulsion of recent Nepali settlers and, in its wilder moments, the recovery of the Duars ceded at Sinchula in 1865. It despises assemblies and foreign advisers alike; its leverage depends on unrest in the south and a weak hand at the palace.

22.name: Royal Bhutan Army
22.text:
Built up after the Chinese occupation of Tibet and trained since 1962 by the Indian Military Training Team, the Royal Bhutan Army guards the northern passes and the southern foothills. Its deputy commander Namgyal Bahadur was executed in 1964 for the murder of Lonchen Jigme Palden Dorji, and since then the army has been led by Lam Dorji, an officer loyal to the throne.

It sees itself as the shield of the dynasty and the frontier, depends on Indian equipment, pay and training, and stays out of politics while the throne is secure. Yet 1964 showed that ambitious officers can make the army an arbiter, and its loyalty remains the ultimate guarantee of whoever rules in Thimphu.

23.name: House of Wangchuck
23.text:
The Wangchuck dynasty has ruled since 1907, when Ugyen Wangchuck was chosen as the first Druk Gyalpo. The third king, Jigme Dorji Wangchuck, on the throne since 1952, has abolished serfdom, created the National Assembly, the Royal Advisory Council and a Council of Ministers, and opened the kingdom to roads, schools and Indian development aid. His heir, Crown Prince Jigme Singye Wangchuck, is fourteen.

The crown pursues reform from above: modernisation without loss of identity, close partnership with India under the 1949 treaty, and full sovereignty through membership of the United Nations. Its authority is personal and near absolute, resting on the army, the blessing of the monk body and the deep loyalty of the valleys.
